sections.title: A practical home for your next app

blocks.text: SoftN brings an editable interface, application logic and local data together in one portable app. Shape an app visually in Builder, describe it to your own AI provider in Studio, or write the source yourself. Runtime opens the result so you can use it.

These guides follow the decisions you actually make: what to build, which tool to open, which language to write logic in, where records live and how to share the app. You do not need to understand a virtual machine before changing a heading.

sections.title: Understand the pieces as you need them

blocks.text: A `.ui` file describes the interface. Logic, written in JavaScript (`.logic` files) or Python (`.py` files), runs in the ZIPP engine. XDB keeps app-scoped records. The host is the browser, desktop application or website that runs the app and decides which capabilities it may use.

A `.softn` bundle carries the editable client. A private backend is a separate deployment. Keeping that line clear makes exports easier to understand and keeps private server material out of downloads.

The guides explain the workflow and the concepts, with small examples. They are not an exhaustive reference for every component property: follow the source links at the end of each page for the underlying files, and check the host you deploy to before relying on an optional capability.

seo.title: What is SoftN? | SoftN Docs
seo.description: What is SoftN? An open-source app platform: portable .softn files, visual and AI-assisted tools, app logic in JavaScript or Python, and browser or desktop hosts.

sections.title: One app you can open, edit and run

blocks.text: SoftN is an open-source UI language, visual builder and runtime for editable apps on the web and desktop. Its portable `.softn` format packages the interface, client logic, data seeds and assets, so an app can be reopened and changed rather than treated as a finished black box.

That gives you several ways to start: explore an existing app, change a project in Builder, describe an idea in Studio with an AI provider you configure, or write the source yourself. These are different routes into the same editable app, not separate product formats.

items.description: The workspace for visual design, source editing, data modelling and previewing an app.
AI-assisted creation. Choose a provider, describe the app in a short brief, approve a plan and review what it generates.
Opens and runs bundles: a browser library at `/web/` and a desktop loader.
The ZIP-based app bundle you can export, share, reopen and customise.

blocks.text: You do not need an AI account to open the Fieldnotes example, start a project in Builder or edit source by hand. AI-assisted generation is one optional way in.

sections.title: From useful forms to interactive experiences

blocks.text: The built-in component library covers layouts, forms, data displays, charts and dashboards. Audio, animation and Three.js scenes extend it to games and richer interactive apps, and a Python app can train small machine-learning models with torch, all subject to what the host supports and grants.

A small planner is a good first app because it exercises input, logic, records and presentation without external services. A connected business dashboard adds another layer: authenticated backend actions, a server database and an access policy.

sections.title: Portable does not mean every host is identical

blocks.text: The bundle carries the editable client. It does not carry a running backend, external credentials, another person’s records or permission grants. A browser host and a desktop host can offer different capabilities.

blocks.title: Keep ownership practical
blocks.text: Keep an exported bundle or a source-controlled project you can restore. Browser storage is useful working storage, but it should not be your only copy of something important.

SoftN, ZIPP and XDB have different jobs. SoftN renders the app and connects its parts; ZIPP runs its logic, in JavaScript or Python; XDB keeps local records. FormLogic is an optional hosted integration, not a prerequisite for a standalone app.

Open Fieldnotes in Builder, change a heading, preview the result and export it. Reopen the export in Runtime. That short loop shows the central promise of the format: the thing you run remains something you can edit.

sections.title: Begin with something that already works

blocks.text: Fieldnotes is the repository’s introductory task planner: its interface is `ui/main.ui`, its JavaScript logic is `logic/main.logic` and its tasks live in an XDB collection. Start there before writing a bundle of your own.

sections.title: A small app you can read end to end

blocks.text: A new Builder project has this shape: an interface in `ui/main.ui` that links its logic file with `<logic src>`, and a counter in that file. The path is relative to the `.ui` file.

blocks.code:
<logic src="../logic/main.logic" />

<App theme="dark">
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Heading level={1}>My first SoftN app</Heading>
    <Text>Count: {count}</Text>
    <Button variant="primary" @click={increment}>Increment</Button>
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: ui/main.ui: the interface, linked to its logic file.
logic/main.logic: state and a function, in JavaScript.

blocks.text: `count` is state. The Text expression displays it. The Button’s `@click` calls `increment`, which changes the state, and SoftN redraws what depends on it.

The same app in Python links `../logic/main.py`. A function that changes a top-level name declares it `global`, and the button calls it through an arrow, because a handler bound by name is passed the click event and a Python function with no parameter for it would fail.

blocks.code:
count = 0


def increment():
    global count
    count = count + 1
blocks.caption: logic/main.py: the same counter in Python.

blocks.code: <Button variant="primary" @click={() => increment()}>Increment</Button>
blocks.caption: In a Python app, call a function with no parameters through an arrow.

blocks.text: Add a reset function that sets `count` to zero, then bind a second Button to it. It uses the same state and event pattern without persistence or networking.

blocks.caption: Add this to logic/main.logic.
Or this to logic/main.py.

blocks.code: <Button @click={() => reset()}>Reset</Button>
blocks.caption: Place this beside the Increment button, inside the Stack. The arrow form works in either language.

blocks.text: A variable here is live app state, not a durable record. Closing and reopening the app is a different test from redrawing it. Use XDB when you are ready to keep records.

seo.title: SoftN Builder | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN Builder: the Design, Data, Preview and Code views, new projects in JavaScript or Python, the logic dock, handler suggestions, torch, permissions and export.

blocks.text: Builder is where you shape an app you can inspect and keep editing. It has four views: Design, a visual canvas with a properties panel; Data, for collections and their seed records; Preview, the running app; and Code, the source of the open file.
Start a project with New, reopen a bundle with Open (Ctrl+O), or open Fieldnotes from the homepage. A visual change is a change to editable source, not a step away from it.

sections.title: Start a project in JavaScript or Python

blocks.text: The Create New App dialog asks for an App Name, a Description, a Theme (Light, Dark or System), a Starter Template (Blank, Landing or Dashboard) and a Logic Language.

items.description: The default. Logic in `.logic` files, in JavaScript.
Logic in `.py` modules. Adds the Machine learning (torch) option, which lets the app import torch; you can change it later in Export.

blocks.text: Either way the project has `ui/main.ui`, linked to its logic with `<logic src>`, a starter counter in the logic file and an empty `assets/` folder. An app uses one language for all its logic.

The Logic dock under the canvas edits the file the active page links with `<logic src>`, in that file’s language: a badge says JavaScript or Python, and the header shows the path. When the page links no logic, the dock shows the entry page’s. Hide it, and Show Logic Panel brings it back.

A page that still keeps its logic inline, in a `<logic>` block, is edited in Code view, and the dock offers Move logic to a file. That moves the block into a linked file and never overwrites a file that already holds other logic. A saved session whose entry page has inline logic is moved the same way when it is restored, when nothing would be lost.

In the properties panel, an event field such as a Button’s click suggests the functions the linked logic file defines, shown as `name(params)`. Choosing a Python function with no parameters inserts `() => name()`, because a handler bound by name is passed the event.
A handler can be any expression. A name the file does not define is kept, with a warning such as “No function named save in logic/main.py.”

items: A path that already exists is refused: “… already exists. Choose another name.” This applies to creating, renaming and moving files and folders.
A `.py` file needs a Python module name: letters, digits and underscores. Reserved module names are refused, with the reason: `softn`, `torch`, `json`, `math` and anything starting `__softn`.
Two `.py` files with the same name in different folders are refused, because Python imports by module name.
Moving a file or renaming a folder rewrites every `<logic src>` that pointed at it.
A logic file created without an extension gets the project’s: `.py` or `.logic`.

items.title: Open or create
items.text: Begin with a known bundle or a new project. Keep a copy before a large structural change.

items.title: Edit the interface
items.text: In Design, select a component and change a property such as Text Content. Check the interaction in Preview, not only the canvas.

items.title: Write the behaviour
items.text: Use the Logic dock or Code view. Keep related changes small enough to test on their own.

items.title: Review the data
items.text: Use the Data view for collections and the seeds the app will carry.

items.title: Preview and export
items.text: Check the sizes you support, export the bundle and reopen that exported copy.

blocks.text: Not every source construct is safe for a canvas to rewrite. Code view marks each file Visual + source or Source-only; a Source-only file is edited as text, which protects its source rather than simplifying it until the canvas accepts it.
Use Design where it offers a clear control, and Code for complex behaviour and structures that do not round-trip through the canvas. After either, run the same user flow again.

Live Preview runs the app at Desktop (1440×900), Tablet (768×1024) or Mobile (390×844). It composes the app the way the runtime does, so a problem Run would refuse, such as an undeclared `import torch`, shows here first; for that one, Preview offers Enable torch.

Preview keeps working while a logic file is open: it runs the entry page and says so. Responsive behaviour still depends on the layout you wrote, so check forms, navigation, long text and tables at the narrowest size you support.

sections.title: Preview data and exported seeds are different jobs

blocks.text: Preview has its own test records, while the Data view holds the seeds the bundle carries. An app that looks populated in Preview may still need careful seeds for a first-time user.

blocks.title: Test a fresh start
blocks.text: Reopen the exported bundle in a clean context and check empty lists, first records and initial settings. That tells you more than repeatedly testing your populated workspace.

Export (Ctrl+Shift+E) opens Export Bundle. What the app may use writes `permission.json`: the capabilities, the allowed hosts for network access and storage policies per collection. For a Python app, a Python section writes `config.python.packages` to `manifest.json`. Then choose Export .softn, Open in runtime… or Publish….
For a first project, stop when one core flow is reliable: create a record, show it, change it and reopen the export. Add polish after that path works.

seo.title: SoftN Studio | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN Studio for AI-assisted app creation: provider presets, the brief, JavaScript or Python logic, torch, the blueprint review, preview, the validator and export.

sections.title: Turn a brief into an editable starting point

blocks.text: Studio is SoftN’s AI-assisted way to create an app. You connect a provider, describe the app, approve a plan, and an AI agent builds it: it reads and edits the files, checks the app after every change and fixes what breaks, until the app does what you asked. The result is ordinary SoftN source you can keep editing.

items.description: A model running on your computer through Ollama, LM Studio or another OpenAI-compatible server. Free and private; the server needs to allow requests from the page (CORS).
Your OpenAI account; OpenAI bills it for what the AI does.
Your Anthropic account; Anthropic bills it for what the AI does.
Any service that accepts the OpenAI chat-completions format, with its address and key.

blocks.text: On a first visit Studio asks you to connect one before anything else. After connecting it lists the provider’s own models for you to choose from, and Test connection explains a failure in plain words (a wrong key, a local server without CORS). The key is kept in this browser’s local storage, not encrypted, and sent only to the provider, straight from the browser. Settings lists your providers and opens the same setup to add or edit one.

AI generation is not required. From the dashboard you can Start a new app, Import a bundle (`.softn`, `.zip` or `.json`) or Start from an example, which needs no key: Reading list, in JavaScript, and Reading list in Python.

The brief has three steps, Basics, Structure and Style, and ends with Generate. Structure is where you choose the Logic language: JavaScript (`.logic`), the default, or Python (`.py`). The whole app uses one language. With Python selected, Uses machine learning `torch` adds torch to `manifest.json`.

A useful description names the people using the app, the records they manage, the screens they need and what each important button does. Say what stays local and which operations, if any, need a backend.

blocks.code:
Create a local task planner for one person.

Screens: task list and a small summary dashboard.
Each task needs a title and completion status.
Let me add a task, mark it complete and filter the list.
Use local records. Do not add login, AI calls or a backend.
Make empty states clear and keep the phone layout readable.
blocks.caption: An example description. It is plain language, not a special command syntax.

blocks.text: Before any code is written, the Blueprint review shows the planned pages, data model, risks and assumptions. Approve blueprint, add a note and revise the plan, or go back with Revise brief. One complete loop is easier to review than many unfinished screens.

sections.title: How the AI builds your app

blocks.text: Approve and build on the blueprint, or any message in the chat, starts a run. The AI works in steps with tools: it lists, reads and searches files, writes a file or makes an exact edit inside one, looks up components and the SoftN guides, checks the app, inspects what the preview shows, and calls the app’s own functions to test that they work. It keeps a short plan you can watch, asks you a question when the brief leaves something open, and finishes with a summary.

After every step that changes files, Studio checks the app the way Run does — the composer, the validator and a real render — and hands any error back, so a mistake is fixed in the next step rather than left for you. A run cannot finish while the check fails.

items: The chat shows the run as a timeline: the plan, each step as a row you can open to see its diff or check report, and the AI’s notes between steps. The preview updates as files change.
Stop ends a run at any point; Continue picks it up again. A network failure pauses the run with Resume rather than losing it.
Every step that writes can be undone on its own, and Revert run undoes the whole run.

A run ends at its step limit or token budget, or after the same failure three times, and says which. Both limits, the automatic check and whether deleting files asks you first are in Settings, under Agent runs.
The AI only reads what it needs, so a large project does not make every request larger. It cannot change a file it has not read in the run, and it cannot write outside the project.

blocks.title: Ask for the result
blocks.text: Describe the result, not the steps: who uses the app, what they record, what each screen and button does. The AI plans the steps and checks its own work, and you can answer its questions as it goes.

The preview composes the app exactly as Run does. When the composer refuses the app, the canvas says “This app cannot be previewed as it stands.” with the reason, naming the file, and a View source expander. An undeclared `import torch` offers Enable torch, which adds torch to `config.python.packages`; Undo takes it back out.

The validator runs the same composer whenever the files or the blueprint change. While it reports a refusal, Run and Publish are disabled (“Fix what the validator found first”); Export bundle stays available, so you can take the files elsewhere to fix them. It also rejects a `.py` file under `server/`: server logic runs as JavaScript on every backend host.

items.title: Try narrow layouts
items.text: Check labels, controls and navigation at phone size.

items.title: Export and reopen
items.text: Check that the project survives the same bundle handoff as a hand-written app.

blocks.text: Import takes a whole bundle. Logic files come in as text, `.py` included, and Export bundle lists `.logic` and `.py` files under `files.logic` in the manifest, leaving server logic out of that group. The export is the same `.softn` format Builder and Runtime open.

An external AI provider can involve its own credentials, limits and charges. Review the configuration and the provider’s terms before sending content. Never put a private access token in app source or a downloadable bundle.

blocks.title: Generation is not validation
blocks.text: Generated logic and UI still need review. A convincing explanation is not proof that a function exists, an export is complete or a permission is granted.
Refine the result in Studio or open the export in Builder. The useful outcome is an app whose behaviour you understand and whose source you can change, not a prompt you can never reproduce.
For a connected app, describe the client and backend responsibilities separately. A generated interface is not, by itself, a deployed authentication system or private API.

pages.title: SoftN Runtime
pages.summary: Open bundles, switch between running apps and understand what the browser library does and does not keep.

seo.title: SoftN Runtime | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN Runtime: open .softn bundles, browse apps, use the saved browser library, switch running apps, and see how it picks the engine for JavaScript or Python logic.

sections.title: The place to use an app

blocks.text: Runtime opens and runs `.softn` bundles. On the web, at `/web/`, it opens a bundle from the + button or a file dropped on the page, runs apps from the directory and keeps a library of what you opened in this browser. The desktop loader is a Tauri app (`npm run dev:desktop` in a checkout).
Creation tools change an app; Runtime uses it. The same bundle can be reopened in Builder or Studio when you want to customise it.

Runtime reads the app before it starts. Logic files ending `.py` make it a Python app, anything else a JavaScript one, and both run in the same ZIPP web-python engine. A bundle the composer refuses, for example one that mixes the two languages or imports torch without declaring it, does not start, and the message says what to change.

sections.title: Home is not the same as Close

blocks.text: The web workspace keeps apps running when you return to its home view, so you can browse or open another app without losing an unfinished form. Use Home to switch between apps and Close to stop the current one.
Test this in your own app. Navigating within a running workspace, closing an app and reopening a saved bundle can involve different state and persistence.

Apps you open are kept in this browser’s library, with offline readiness shown for saved apps. That is not an account-wide backup: another device, another browser profile or cleared site storage can have different contents.

blocks.title: Check offline readiness before relying on it
blocks.text: A saved app may still use network services or remote resources. Test the real workflow without a connection, and keep a separate copy of important exports.

sections.title: The host decides what the app can reach

blocks.text: A capability needs support and permission from the host. The browser can also ask for its own consent for camera or microphone access. A desktop build may offer native storage or integrations an ordinary browser cannot.
The manifest name is not a storage account. The general bundle loader, single-app deployments and FormLogic each have identity rules that decide which records and grants an app sees.

items: Open the exported bundle, not only the editor preview.
Exercise the main flow, and return Home without losing unfinished input.
Close and reopen, then check which state is meant to persist.
Review permission requests, and test denial as well as approval.
Confirm the host and browser you actually plan to support.

blocks.text: When something differs between preview and Runtime, first work out whether the difference is UI state, data seeds, persistent records, host capability support or deployment configuration.

pages.title: The .softn app format
pages.summary: What a bundle contains, how its manifest configures logic and packages, what an export leaves behind, and how to think about seeds and permissions.

seo.title: The .softn app format | SoftN Docs
seo.description: The .softn format: a ZIP bundle with manifest.json, permission.json, UI, JavaScript or Python logic, XDB seeds and assets; config.execution and config.python.packages.

blocks.text: A `.softn` file is a ZIP-based app bundle holding the editable client material SoftN needs to load an app. It is the handoff between creation tools and runtimes: export an app, reopen it and change its source.
It does not contain every external dependency. A remote service, an AI provider or a private server database keeps its own deployment and access requirements.

blocks.code:
my-app.softn
├── manifest.json
├── permission.json
├── ui/
├── logic/
├── xdb/
└── assets/
blocks.caption: The layout Builder and Studio write. Exact files depend on the app.

items.description: App metadata, the entry file and optional configuration.
The capabilities the app requests from its host. Declaring one is not the same as being granted it.
The interface: `.ui` files.
Client logic: `.logic` files in JavaScript, or `.py` files in Python. One language per app.
Optional collection seeds carried with the app.
Images, styles, sounds, models and other distributable files.

blocks.text: `manifest.json` needs a `name` and a `main` entry, the path of the interface file that opens first; the rest is optional for opening an app. A `files` section listing the `ui`, `logic`, `xdb` and `assets` entries is conventional and is what the editors write, but a bundle without it still opens. The app directory’s publication check also asks for a `version` and warns when there is no `description`. `permission.json` is optional too: without it the app asks for nothing.

blocks.caption: A Python app that uses torch. Both config keys are optional.

items.description: `"main"`, the default, runs logic on the page’s thread; `"worker"` asks for a JavaScript app’s logic to run in a worker. Python logic always runs on the main thread. Any other value is reported and treated as main.
The Python packages the app imports. `torch` is the only one offered; any other name is refused. An `import torch` the manifest does not declare is refused too, with the line to add.
Lists `.logic` or `.py` files, never both. The file name alone decides the language.

items: A logic file whose name ends `.py` is Python; any other is JavaScript. Nothing else declares the language.
A bundle that mixes Python and JavaScript logic is refused: the two run in separate engines and cannot share names.
Python must live in a file referenced with `<logic src>`. An inline `<logic lang="python">` block is refused, because reindenting markup could change the program.
Each `.py` file is a module named after the file, so two with the same name are refused, and the names `softn`, `torch`, `json`, `math` and anything starting `__softn` are reserved.
Server logic for the PHP and Rust hosts is JavaScript. Python is client logic only.

sections.title: Seeds are not a backup of live records

blocks.text: Seed records are starting content for a new app instance. The records someone creates while using the app belong to that host’s storage and identity rules. Exporting a project does not export every user’s live database.

Builder’s preview uses test records. Review the seeds you mean to distribute in the Data view, then test a fresh runtime instance, so a demo does not look complete only because it is using your local data.

sections.title: Separate client downloads from private deployment

blocks.text: Server hosts can run server-side `.logic` resources. The browser never executes those, and a backend deployment decides how to keep private scripts, credentials and SQLite databases on the server.

blocks.title: Assume a recipient can inspect the bundle
blocks.text: Anything in a downloadable client archive should be something you intend to share. An editable client bundle cannot hide a service secret or a private database.

sections.title: Identity and compatibility belong to the host too

blocks.text: The general bundle loader isolates bundles by digest. Single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own deployment identity. An app name alone does not grant access to another app’s records or permission grants.
Test a bundle on the host you intend to use. A successful export confirms packaging, not browser microphone consent, backend authorisation or support for every optional capability.

pages.title: The SoftN UI language
pages.summary: Read component tags, expressions, bindings, event handlers and control flow, and link a page to its logic file.

seo.title: The SoftN UI language | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN .ui syntax: components, expression props, event handlers and their arguments, two-way binding, conditional and list rendering, and linking logic files.

blocks.text: A `.ui` file describes the interface with component tags, properties and expressions. SoftN parses the source and renders it through React, but the app source is SoftN syntax: you do not rewrite it as JSX.

A page links its logic with `<logic src="../logic/main.logic" />`, a path relative to the `.ui` file; a Python app links a `.py` file the same way. JavaScript can also sit inline in a `<logic>` block; Python cannot.

blocks.code:
<Button variant="primary" size="md">Save</Button>
<Text>{message}</Text>
<Text color={isDark ? "white" : "black"}>{message}</Text>
blocks.caption: Literal properties and brace-delimited expressions.

blocks.text: Quoted values are literal strings. Braces hold expressions whose values come from the app’s state. Keep expressions simple and move complicated decisions into named logic functions.

blocks.code:
<Input :bind={username} placeholder="Enter your name" />
<Button @click={save}>Save</Button>
<Button @click={() => clear()}>Clear</Button>
blocks.caption: The username state and the save and clear functions are defined in the app’s logic.

blocks.text: `:bind` is two-way: what the person types is written back to the state variable. Any other `:` property, such as `:value={x}`, only shows the value. `@click` and the other `@` events call a handler.

A handler bound by name receives an argument: for most events, a plain-data summary of the browser event, and for `@change` and `@input`, the new value. It is never the live DOM event, so there is no `preventDefault` or `event.target`. Write an arrow, `@click={() => save()}`, to call a function without it; Python apps need that form for functions with no parameters.

blocks.code:
#if (isLoggedIn)
  <Text>Welcome back</Text>
#else
  <Text>Please sign in</Text>
#end

#each (task in tasks)
  <Text>{task.title}</Text>
#empty
  <Text>No tasks yet</Text>
#end
blocks.caption: Control flow over app state. Here tasks is an ordinary list of objects with a title field.

blocks.text: `#elseif (…)` adds further branches. An `#empty` branch makes the first-run experience explicit, which is kinder than a blank area that leaves someone wondering whether the app has loaded.

Use layout components for structure, display components for readable content and form components for actions and input. `asset("assets/cover.png")` resolves a file inside the bundle, and reusable app components keep repeated sections consistent.

blocks.title: Keep the first screen readable
blocks.text: A heading, a short explanation, one input and one action are enough to test a complete interaction before you add navigation and dashboards.

pages.title: App logic in JavaScript or Python
pages.summary: Write an app’s behaviour in JavaScript or Python, see what the two share, and understand the ZIPP engine and the host APIs around it.

seo.title: App logic in JavaScript or Python | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN app logic with ZIPP: JavaScript .logic or Python .py files, one language per app, the shared state and handler contract, the WebAssembly engine and host bridges.

blocks.text: An app’s logic is JavaScript in `.logic` files or Python in `.py` files. Both run in ZIPP, an engine written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly for the browser. The file name decides the language, and an app uses one language for all its logic: a bundle that mixes them is refused.

The engine runs the language; SoftN supplies the app integration: state, rendering and the host APIs it chooses to expose. Knowing JavaScript or Python does not mean every browser global, Node.js module, npm package or pip package is available.

rows: Top-level names; a leading `_` keeps one private
Declare it `global` in the function, then assign it
blocks.caption: The same app can be written in either language; these are the differences that show.
JavaScript: load records at startup, then refresh the state the interface reads after each change.

blocks.code:
tasks = []
draft = ""


def add_task():
    global tasks, draft
    title = draft.strip()
    if title == "":
        return
    tasks = tasks + [{"title": title, "done": False}]
    draft = ""
blocks.caption: Python: bind the input with :bind={draft} and the button with @click={() => add_task()}.

blocks.text: Both follow the same pattern: an action changes state explicitly, and the interface redraws from it. That is easier to trace than data changes hidden inside a display expression.

sections.title: The engine and the host are separate layers

blocks.text: ZIPP’s browser build is an interpreter inside WebAssembly. The upstream project’s native JIT tiers are not what runs in the browser, so native benchmark results are not SoftN browser performance.

The host decides what a script can call. Bridges such as `db` and `softn.*` are gated by the app’s declarations and the host’s grants, and a Python app’s calls go through the same checks. A bridge existing is no reason to assume unrestricted access.

blocks.title: The page is outside the guest
blocks.text: Logic is guest code in the environment the host gives it, not a script tag with access to the whole page.

SoftN ships ZIPP v0.0.21’s web-python-base release build: JavaScript and Python in one WebAssembly module (7.46 MB, about 1.7 MB compressed), without torch. ZIPP’s verified web-torch package is installed beside it and loaded only for apps that declare torch. Neither is committed to the repository. `npm run fetch:zipp`, and the build and test scripts when it is missing, install the release named by the `zipp-vm` tag in `apps/softn-host-rust/Cargo.toml`, check it against that release’s SHA256SUMS and record its provenance in SOURCE.json.
Rebuilding the engine is a separate maintenance task with its own Rust and WebAssembly tooling; ordinary SoftN development never needs it.
The PHP and Rust hosts run server-side `.logic` as JavaScript. Python is for client logic: a `.py` file under `server/` would never run, and Studio’s validator says so.

sections.title: Learn the boundaries before adding integrations

blocks.text: Start with app state and records. When you add networking, media, GPU work or backend actions, read the relevant capability guide and test both the allowed and the denied path. A working expression proves less than a complete user flow.

pages.title: State, events and app lifecycle
pages.summary: Connect user actions to state, understand event data, and distinguish a running screen from durable records.

seo.title: State, events and app lifecycle | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN state and events: handlers and the plain-data event they receive, two-way binding, keyboard and pointer input in JavaScript and Python, and state versus saved records.

sections.title: State connects behaviour to the interface

blocks.text: The top-level names in an app’s logic are its state. SoftN mirrors them into the renderer around each call into the logic, so a change made by an action shows up in every expression that reads it.

For a small app, keep important state obvious: a current filter, a form field, the records shown in a list or the selected item. Change it with named actions, so a click can be traced from the template to the function and back to the screen.

A handler bound by name, such as `@click={save}`, is called with whatever the component passes. For a browser event that is a plain-data summary: the type, pointer position and buttons, modifier keys and the target’s tag. It is never the live DOM event, so `event.preventDefault()` and `event.target` are not available.

`@change` and `@input` pass the new value instead. Other components pass their own data: DPad’s `@press` gives the direction and Slider’s `@change` the number. Check what the component you use passes before writing logic around it.

blocks.code:
<Input :bind={username} placeholder="Name" />
<Button @click={() => save()}>Save</Button>
blocks.caption: Read the bound username state inside save. The arrow calls save with no argument, which suits a Python function with no parameters.

blocks.text: For keys and pointers anywhere on the page, JavaScript logic uses `window.addEventListener` and Python logic uses `softn.on("keydown", handler)`. Either way the listener receives plain data, such as `key`, `code`, `clientX`, `clientY` and `targetTag`, not a browser object.
Box and Button forward pointerdown, pointerup, pointercancel and pointerleave, for controls that react while held. Handle cancellation and leaving the control, not only the first press.

blocks.code: softn.input.captureKeys(["ArrowUp", " ", "F1"])
blocks.caption: Keys the app captures from the page. The host still protects text fields, Ctrl combinations and the system modifier.

blocks.text: Capture only the keys the app needs. A game should not make it hard to type into its own settings form or use familiar browser shortcuts.

rows: Does the interface update after an action?
Does unfinished input survive returning Home and switching apps?
Does the data you meant to keep survive closing and reopening the app?
blocks.caption: Separate acceptance checks, not interchangeable definitions of persistence.

blocks.text: `_init()` runs once when the app loads, in either language. Use XDB for records: a counter or selected tab is not a database record. Decide which state should restart and which should be restored.

sections.title: Trace one interaction at a time

items.title: Check the binding
items.text: Confirm the template names the function and state you intended, and in Python that a handler without parameters is called through an arrow.

items.title: Check the function
items.text: Reduce it to one state change before adding database or network work. In Python, check the `global` line.

items.title: Check the host boundary
items.text: Permission, capability support and backend availability can fail independently of the UI.

items.title: Check the lifecycle
items.text: Find out whether the problem appears after a redraw, an app switch, a close or a fresh open.

pages.title: SoftN component guide
pages.summary: Find a sensible starting component for layouts, forms, data, charts, media, animation and richer apps.

seo.title: SoftN component guide | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Explore SoftN components for layouts, forms, tables, dashboards, charts, media, animation, editors and Three.js scenes.

sections.title: Choose a component by the job it does

blocks.text: The built-in library is organised into layout, form, display, feedback, data, navigation, utility, chart, animation, editor, 3D and smart components. Start with the role you need rather than a list of every property.

This is a guide to finding a component, not a complete property reference. Every name below is registered in `@softn/components`; for exact properties and callback values, read a working example or the component’s source.

rows: App, Box, Stack, Grid, Card, Container, Layout, Header, Content, Section
Text, Heading, Badge, Tag, Progress, Spinner, Image, Icon
Button, Input, TextArea, Select, Checkbox, Radio, Switch, Form, Slider
Alert, Modal, Toast, Drawer, Popover, EmptyState
blocks.caption: A starting selection from the component library.

blocks.text: Choose the simplest component that matches the interaction. A small settings screen may need only a Stack, Heading, Input and Button. More components do not necessarily make the workflow clearer.

rows: List, ListItem, Table, DataGrid, TreeView, Pagination
LineChart, BarChart, PieChart, AreaChart, RadarChart, GaugeChart
blocks.caption: Smart components offer data-driven configuration; ordinary components give you more direct presentation control.

blocks.text: Use a table when someone needs to inspect individual records. Use a chart for a question about a pattern or comparison. A chart is most useful when its labels, units and empty state make that question understandable.

The library also includes PixelGrid, PixelCanvas, QRCode, QRReader, Camera, Microphone, AudioStream and DPad; animation components such as AnimatedBox, AnimatedNumber, Sprite and TileMap; editors such as CodeEditor, MarkdownEditor and RichTextEditor; and Scene3D for Three.js scenes.

Their presence in the library does not remove browser constraints or host permissions. Media input and advanced host integrations should be checked in the actual deployment, not only in a component catalogue.

items.title: Find a working example
items.text: Start with a bundle that already uses the component for the same kind of task.

pages.title: Forms, tables and dashboards
pages.summary: Build a useful record workflow before adding extra screens, summaries and visual polish.

seo.title: Forms, tables and dashboards | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Build SoftN forms, tables and dashboards with XDB, SmartForm, SmartGrid and clear record workflows, validation and empty states.

blocks.text: A record-oriented app usually needs a small loop: enter information, save it, show the result and update it later. Build that loop before adding several dashboards. It makes the relationship between the interface, logic and data easier to test.
SoftN offers ordinary form and data components, and smart components configured by collection. Choose whichever makes your app’s behaviour easiest to explain.

blocks.code:
<SmartForm
  collection="clients"
  fields="name:text:required, email:email:required, phone:text"
  submitText="Add Client"
/>
blocks.caption: A SmartForm for a clients collection. The app supplies the collection.

blocks.text: The example identifies the collection and fields, including required name and email inputs. Treat validation at the UI as help for the user, not a substitute for checks on a private backend that accepts submitted data.
Decide what happens after a save: clear the form, keep values for a similar next record, show a confirmation or return to a list. Test that the user can tell whether the operation succeeded.

blocks.code:
<SmartGrid
  collection="clients"
  columns="name, email, phone, visits"
  searchable sortable pageable
/>
blocks.caption: A read-oriented SmartGrid. Add editing only after defining and testing the update flow.

blocks.text: Choose columns for the task, not merely because the fields exist. Long text and too many columns can make a phone layout difficult. A list or card layout may be a better small-screen view.

sections.title: Add summaries that answer a question

blocks.text: SmartStats, chart components and ordinary display components can turn records into a dashboard. Give each summary a clear meaning: open tasks, visits during a period or records needing follow-up. Label the time window and units where they matter.
Compute summaries from the same intended records as the list. A dashboard and table that disagree may be using different filters, stale state or preview data instead of the live collection.

items: Start with no records and confirm the next action is clear.
Submit incomplete or invalid values and check the explanation.
Create a record and confirm it appears in the view.
Update a record and verify totals and filters still agree.
Reopen the app and check the intended persistence.
Check phone-sized layouts and keyboard access.

blocks.text: When the flow needs shared authenticated records, add a backend deliberately. Local XDB storage and server authorisation solve different problems.

pages.title: Local app data with XDB
pages.summary: Understand collections, record operations, seeds, app identity and optional synchronisation.

seo.title: Local app data with XDB | SoftN Docs
seo.description: XDB in SoftN: local collections, the synchronous db bridge, bundle seeds, app-scoped storage, host-dependent sync, and what Python apps use instead of db.

blocks.text: XDB is SoftN’s local-first data layer. It keeps app-scoped records and gives JavaScript logic a `db` bridge with synchronous operations over an in-memory cache; how records persist, and whether native storage is used, depends on the host.
Think of a collection as records of one kind, such as clients or tasks. Think separately about its schema, its starting seed records and the live records someone creates while using the app.

blocks.title: Python apps
blocks.text: `db` is a JavaScript global. Python logic has no `db`; it can use `softn.storage.*` for the app’s server storage, which needs the storage capability.

blocks.caption: Create, query, update and delete. Skip the last line if you want to keep the record.

blocks.text: Create and query name a collection; update and delete take a record id. The full `db` surface:

items.description: One record, or null when it does not exist.
The records of a collection, optionally those matching the given field values.
Adds a record and returns it with its id.
Merges the patch into the record and returns the result.
Marks the record deleted, so sync peers learn about it.
Removes the record outright, without a tombstone.
Keeps the newest maxRecords records and returns how many were removed.
Removes every record of the collection.
Optional peer synchronisation; see below.

blocks.text: For a reactive screen, make it clear when the state the UI shows is refreshed. The usual pattern queries records in `_init()` and queries again after each change.

Builder’s Data view shows each collection’s structure and seed records. Use the schema to make field intent clear, and ship only seeds that suit every recipient. Do not distribute a real customer dataset because it made a convincing local demo.

blocks.title: Preview is not the exported database
blocks.text: Builder’s preview has its own test records. Review the seeds in the Data view and test a fresh app instance before assuming the export holds the intended starting data.

sections.title: App identity is not just a display name

blocks.text: The general loader isolates bundles by digest, while single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own identity. A display name alone is no authority to read another app’s data.
Treat upgrades and moves between hosts as data-lifecycle decisions. Before changing an identity or deployment, test which records remain available and keep a recovery copy suited to that host.

blocks.code: await db.startSync('my-room-name')
blocks.caption: Start peer synchronisation. The host must support it and the app needs the sync capability.

blocks.text: A room name is not an authentication or privacy policy. Decide who may take part, how access is controlled and what the host provides before using sync for sensitive or multi-user records.
Local persistence, peer-to-peer sync and a private server database are not interchangeable. Choose the one that matches the app’s ownership, sharing and recovery needs.

pages.title: Assets, themes and responsive layouts
pages.summary: Keep an app readable, portable and testable across sizes without relying on your own browser cache.

seo.title: Assets, themes and responsive layouts | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Manage SoftN assets, light and dark themes, and responsive layouts. Test exported bundles, narrow screens and fresh app instances.

sections.title: Keep distributable assets with the app

blocks.text: A bundle’s `assets/` folder holds images, styles, sounds, models and other resources. In markup, `asset()` resolves a path inside the bundle, and the audio API resolves bundle paths the same way.

A local file that exists only on your development machine is not automatically part of the exported app. Reopen the exported bundle in a fresh context to catch missing resources that your current preview or browser cache may hide.

blocks.code: <Image src={asset("assets/cover.png")} />
blocks.caption: The asset helper with an Image component. Include the file in the app.

sections.title: Design for the theme you support

blocks.text: The App component takes a `theme`, and Builder’s new projects offer Light, Dark or System. Fieldnotes shows one app drawn in both palettes, and the runtime switches theme without clearing unfinished input.

Test your own colours in each supported theme. A hard-coded text colour that works on one background can become unreadable on another. Use meaning, labels and shape as well as colour to communicate status.

sections.title: A preview size is a test case

blocks.text: Builder previews Desktop, Tablet and Mobile sizes, but responsive behaviour is still part of the layout you wrote. Switching size does not redesign an overflowing table or a navigation bar with too many items.

Keep important controls reachable without horizontal scrolling.

blocks.text: A remote image, font, audio file or model makes the app depend on a network service even when its records are local. Decide whether the asset should be bundled, fetched when needed or treated as optional.

For an app that must work offline, test after the host reports the saved app ready, then disable the connection and exercise the real workflow. The word local-first does not automatically package a remote resource.

pages.title: How SoftN, ZIPP and XDB fit together
pages.summary: A readable map of the interface, guest logic, data and hosting responsibilities.

seo.title: How SoftN, ZIPP and XDB fit together | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN architecture: .ui rendered through React, JavaScript or Python logic in the ZIPP WebAssembly engine, the source composer, XDB records and optional backend hosts.

sections.title: A small map of the platform

blocks.text: SoftN connects an editable UI language, application logic and records. It is easiest to understand with the renderer, the script engine, the database and the host kept as separate responsibilities.

blocks.code:
Editable .softn client bundle
  |
  +-- .ui source ----------> SoftN parser / renderer --> React interface
  |
  +-- .logic or .py -------> ZIPP (WebAssembly) -------> app behaviour
  |
  +-- XDB seeds and assets

The source composer checks and joins the pieces before anything runs.
Host integration connects behaviour to app-scoped records
and to explicitly supported, granted capabilities.

Optional private backend
  authenticated actions --> server logic (JavaScript) / server database
blocks.caption: A responsibility map. A backend is separate from the public client download.

blocks.text: A lexer, parser and renderer turn `.ui` source into React elements through a component registry. Properties and template expressions connect the visible interface to the app’s state.
Authors work in SoftN’s source format. React is part of the host’s rendering, not a separate React project every app author maintains.

Before an app runs, the source composer resolves each page’s `<logic src>`, decides the language from the file names and checks the rules: one language per app, Python in files, valid and unique module names, declared packages. Builder’s preview, Studio’s preview and validator, and Runtime all use the same composer, so a refusal appears in the editor before Run.

ZIPP compiles JavaScript or Python to register bytecode and runs it. In the browser, the WebAssembly build uses its interpreter rather than the native JIT tiers. SoftN’s engine is ZIPP’s web-python-base build, which carries both languages in one module, with torch added as a separate package only when an app declares it; a JavaScript app and a Python app use separate engine instances.

SoftN mirrors the logic’s top-level state into the renderer around each call and supplies host bridges. That is why a button handler can change a variable and redraw an expression without receiving access to the whole browser environment.

XDB supplies app-scoped local records. Bundle seeds provide starting content, while the host controls persistence and identity. Optional sync and native storage depend on what the host supports and allows.
A private SQLite database on a server is a different resource with different access rules. A client can request named backend operations without receiving that database or its credentials.

Builder, Studio and Runtime work with the same editable bundle, while a browser, the desktop loader or a configured website provides the execution environment. FormLogic is an optional connected host with its own authenticated backend.

blocks.title: A shared engine is not shared authority
blocks.text: Hosts can reuse verified engine bytes while each worker or app keeps its own instance, memory and permissions. Reusing an artifact does not share a running VM or grant access between apps.

seo.title: Audio, microphone and media | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Use audio and media in SoftN: sound playback from logic, browser autoplay rules, microphone and camera permissions, and how to test them.

blocks.text: Logic plays sound with `softn.audio`, in JavaScript or, after `import softn`, in Python. Asset paths are resolved inside the bundle. Playback is not microphone capture: playing a bundled sound reads nothing from the microphone.

blocks.caption: Playback calls in JavaScript. Declare themeHandle in your app state and include both audio files.

blocks.text: `setVolume` scales current and later playback, and `whenEnded(handle, callback)` reports when a sound finishes. The runtime stops the audio an app started when that app closes.

Browsers can refuse playback before the person interacts with the page. A one-shot sound then reports `played: false` and `blocked: true`. A looped track reports `pending: true` with its handle and starts on the first click or keystroke.
Design the first screen so sound is optional rather than the only explanation of what is happening. A visible Start action is easier to understand than an app that depends on immediate audio.

blocks.title: Test on a fresh page
blocks.text: A browser that has already received your clicks is not a useful test of the first-visit autoplay path.

blocks.text: The component library includes Camera, Microphone and AudioStream. Capture needs host support and the camera or mic capability, and the browser may also ask the person for consent.
The audio playback API is not permission-gated in the same way as microphone capture. Do not broaden an app’s requested capabilities merely to play a bundled sound effect.

blocks.title: Ask only when the feature needs it
blocks.text: Explain what capture is for and provide a useful denied-permission state. Do not silently upload captured material or embed private service credentials in the client.

Check that playback and capture stop at the intended point.

Keep the game’s responsibilities clear. The scene displays the world; controls capture player intent; .logic updates the app’s state; and the host provides supported capabilities. A settings panel or task list can use ordinary UI components around the scene.

seo.title: Machine learning with torch | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Use torch in a SoftN Python app: declare it in manifest.json, train tensors and torch.nn models on the CPU in the browser, show results as state and keep the page responsive.

sections.title: Models that train in the page

blocks.text: A Python app can use ZIPP’s torch: tensors, autograd, `torch.nn` modules, losses and optimizers, running on the CPU inside the engine. Training happens in the visitor’s browser, with no server, account, network access or permission, and the data and model stay on the device.
It suits small models you can train in seconds: fitting a curve, a tiny classifier, a demonstration of gradient descent. It is not a GPU training environment.

blocks.caption: manifest.json: an app that imports torch says so.

blocks.text: Builder offers this as Machine learning (torch) when you create a Python project, and in the Python section of Export. Studio’s brief offers Uses machine learning `torch`. Either preview offers Enable torch if the app imports torch without the declaration.

items: An `import torch` the manifest does not declare is refused with the line to add: “logic/main.py imports torch, which an app asks for in manifest.json: "config": { "python": { "packages": ["torch"] } }”.
A package the runtime does not offer is refused too. torch is the only one.
`torch.py` is a reserved module name: an app file of that name would hide the package.

sections.title: A model in a few lines

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

xs = torch.tensor([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
ys = xs * 2.0 + 1.0
model = nn.Linear(1, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
loss = 0.0


def train(steps):
    global loss
    for _ in range(steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        current = ((model(xs) - ys) ** 2).mean()
        current.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        loss = float(current)
blocks.caption: logic/main.py: a one-neuron network learns y = 2x + 1.

blocks.code:
<logic src="../logic/main.py" />

<App>
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Text>Loss: {loss}</Text>
    <Button variant="primary" @click={() => train(50)}>Train 50 steps</Button>
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: ui/main.ui: each click trains a short batch and shows the loss.

sections.title: Keep tensors in Python, show numbers

blocks.text: Tensors, models and optimizers are Python objects, so they stay in Python and are never mirrored as state. Keep what the markup shows in plain numbers, strings and lists, such as `loss = float(current)` or a rounded weight, and those update the interface like any other state.

The first `import torch` compiles torch’s Python modules: about a second on a desktop, once per page. A training step of a small model takes a few tens of milliseconds and runs on the page’s thread, so train in short calls, from a button or a timer, rather than one long loop that freezes the page.

items: Eager CPU tensors only. `torch.compile`’s GPU path is not connected in SoftN’s Python runtime, so do not use it.
torch here is ZIPP’s own subset of the PyTorch API, not PyTorch itself. The TORCH_COMPATIBILITY.md file in ZIPP’s release bundles lists what it covers.

The first declaring app on a page also downloads the torch package, about 2 MB (about 380 KB compressed), once; the runtime adds it before the app compiles, and every later torch app on the page reuses it. Apps that do not declare torch never download it. If the package cannot be loaded, the app is refused by name with the reason, rather than failing at its first import.
Python’s own limits apply: no `async`, main thread only, and state must be JSON data.

blocks.text: `examples/torch-trainer` in the repository trains `nn.Linear` to learn y = 2x + 1 from five points, showing the loss, the learned weight and bias, and a prediction as you train. Build it with `node examples/torch-trainer/build.mjs`, then open `TorchTrainer.softn` in the runtime at `/web/` with the + button, or drop the file on the page.

pages.summary: Understand requested capabilities, host grants, browser consent and the limits of an editable client bundle.

seo.title: Permissions and sandboxing | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand SoftN permissions and sandboxing: permission.json, host grants, network allowlists, browser consent and private client-server boundaries.

sections.title: Three questions before an app uses a capability

blocks.text: A useful way to reason about a host operation is to ask: does the app declare it, does this host support and grant it, and does the surrounding browser or service allow it? Those checks can fail independently.
The runtime knows ten capabilities. Each is off until the bundle declares it and the visitor or host grants it, whichever language the app’s logic is written in.

items.description: Network: may call the internet, limited to allowed_hosts; the runtime asks first.
May take pictures, with the visitor’s permission.
May record audio, with the visitor’s permission.
May read files the visitor chooses and save files it makes.
Scans QR codes with the camera.
Downloads and runs a model in the browser.
Uses the graphics card for compute.
Replicates data to the visitor’s other devices and to peers.
Server storage: keeps records in the app’s own database on the hosting site, shared with everyone running the app unless a collection’s policy says otherwise.
Host acceleration: runs the numeric code it generates on the browser’s own engine, bound to its own data.

blocks.caption: A network permission. api.example.com is a placeholder, not a service SoftN provides.

blocks.text: A declaration requests a capability. It does not authenticate to that API, grant server-side access or prove that a destination is appropriate. Use the smallest set of destinations and operations the app needs.
Treat permission.json as part of the app’s public explanation. Someone opening the bundle should be able to understand why a task planner or media app needs each requested capability.

sections.title: The host boundary is part of the design

blocks.text: Guest logic runs in the ZIPP WebAssembly engine and reaches only the integration points SoftN exposes. ZIPP’s host calls are denied by default, and installing a bridge is not the same as granting authority. Python’s `softn.*` calls go through the same host checks as JavaScript’s.

Sandboxing is an implementation boundary, not a promise that every app or host is risk-free. Host code, app data handling, resource limits and private backend authorisation still need appropriate testing.

blocks.title: No client-side hiding place for secrets
blocks.text: A .softn bundle is editable, inspectable source. Keep service credentials and private server databases in a deployment designed to keep them on the server.

A friendly app name is a label, not a storage credential. General bundle loading uses digest-based isolation; configured single-app and FormLogic hosts use their own deployment identity. Test what happens to data and grants when publishing an update.

blocks.text: These pages describe the capability model. They do not certify a deployment’s security or say that any particular host configuration is safe for sensitive records. Review the version, host policy and backend you actually run before deciding that.

Test the actual app flow offline, not only whether its first screen opens. A form might be local while its submit action or background image still depends on a server.

pages.title: Python logic
pages.summary: Write an app’s client logic in Python: link a .py file, keep state in top-level names, change it with global, and call host capabilities through import softn.

seo.title: Python logic | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Write SoftN app logic in Python: .py files, state and global, handlers, modules, import softn, what Python lacks, reserved names and the refusals that explain them.

blocks.text: An app’s client logic can be Python instead of JavaScript. In Builder, choose Python (logic/main.py) as the Logic Language of a new project; in Studio, choose Python in the brief. Or write the file yourself: a logic file whose name ends `.py` is Python, and nothing else says so.

blocks.code:
<logic src="../logic/main.py" />

<App>
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Input :bind={draft} placeholder="New task" />
    <Button variant="primary" @click={() => add_task()}>Add</Button>
    #each (task in tasks)
      <Text>{task.title}</Text>
    #end
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: ui/main.ui links its Python module with <logic src>.

blocks.text: Python must be in a file. An inline `<logic lang="python">` block is refused, because Python’s indentation is the program and markup indentation is not reliable. An app uses one language for all its logic.

items.description: A module-level `count = 0` is state the template can read, like a JavaScript `let`. A name starting with `_` is private to the module.
A function that assigns a module-level name must declare it `global`, or Python creates a local and the state never changes. This is the most common surprise when porting from JavaScript.
Every top-level function can be called from the template. `_init()` runs once after the app loads.
`logic/helpers.py` is the module `helpers`; another file reaches it with `import helpers` or `from helpers import double`.

`dict`, `list`, `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool` and `None`. A class instance, tensor or model stays in Python. Integers beyond ±(2⁵³−1) are shown as strings, non-finite floats as `None`, and state is mirrored about thirty levels deep.
A traceback names your own file and line; the runtime’s generated files are left out.

blocks.text: A handler bound by name is passed the event, so `@click={add_task}` calls `add_task(event)`, and a `def` with no parameter for it raises `TypeError`. Bind it through an arrow, `@click={() => add_task()}`, or give the function a parameter. Builder’s handler suggestions insert the arrow form for you.
Inputs write back to state with `:bind={draft}`. `:value={draft}` only shows the value, so typing would never reach your logic.

`import softn` gives Python the capabilities the JavaScript `softn` global offers, under both Python and JavaScript names (`softn.camera.capture_photo` and `softn.camera.capturePhoto`). Capabilities are asynchronous, so each one takes a callback rather than returning its answer.

blocks.code:
import softn

status = ""


def on_saved(response):
    global status
    status = "Saved"


def save(record):
    softn.backend.call("save", record, on_saved)


def on_key(event):
    global status
    status = "Pressed " + event["key"]


softn.on("keydown", on_key)
blocks.caption: A capability hands its answer to a callback; softn.on registers an event listener.

blocks.text: A value passed to `softn.*` must be JSON data. Anything else raises an error rather than being quietly replaced, so a capability call never sends something other than what you wrote.

items: `db.*`, `localStorage` and `navigator.clipboard`: they are JavaScript globals. Use `softn.storage.*` for the app’s server storage.
`$:` computed declarations, and any template expression that must be evaluated inside the app’s scope. Call a function instead.
Worker execution. A Python app runs on the page’s main thread.
Server logic. The PHP and Rust hosts run server `.logic` as JavaScript.
`async` and `await`, and the other gaps of ZIPP’s Python subset. It is ZIPP’s own implementation of Python, not CPython, and installs no pip packages; torch is the one package the runtime provides.

rows: A `.py` name that is not a Python identifier
Python imports a module by its name
The app, the runtime or the torch package already uses that module name
Two `.py` files with the same name
Each module needs its own name
Python lives in a file the bundle carries verbatim
Python and JavaScript logic in one app
They run in separate engines and cannot share names
The manifest declares every package the app imports
blocks.caption: Builder, Studio and Runtime all compose apps the same way, so each refusal appears before the app runs.

blocks.text: Only ZIPP’s Python builds run Python; SoftN ships web-python-base everywhere. A host that loads the JavaScript-only `zipp-web` engine, such as a FormLogic workspace whose owner chose the smaller engine, refuses a Python app by name before it compiles a line.

seo.description: Host a SoftN app on its own website with the single-app runtime: the build and package commands, every runtime.config.json field, permission modes, identity and the archive variants.

sections.title: A website focused on one app

blocks.text: The single-app runtime (apps/softn-single) is a separate entry point that uses the real renderer, component registry, ZIPP sandbox and XDB, and nothing else: no launcher, catalogue, editor, account bar, bundle cache or download controls. Its loader is a spinner, its title comes from configuration, and the shell carries no product branding. Your app’s own interface renders unchanged.
The app remains a SoftN client. Its editable interface and logic are still distinct from any private service it calls, and a custom domain does not change what is delivered to the browser.

blocks.code:
npm ci
npm run build:single
npm run package:single
blocks.caption: Builds the shared packages and the @softn/single workspace, then writes release/softn-app-static-v<version>.zip. Add `-- --with-backend` to also produce the Apache/PHP backend variant.

blocks.text: Upload the contents of the archive to an HTTPS web directory, at the root or in a subdirectory, keeping the adjacent assets paths intact. PHP, the directory API and a service worker are not required. Serve .wasm as application/wasm and .mjs as JavaScript; the included Apache file sets those types and disables directory listing. Other servers need the equivalent MIME settings.
Every release archive starts with a README.md that says what the package is and how to deploy it, and carries the detailed guide beside it.

items.label: Single-app runtime guide
items.description: The repository guide: limits, the preapproved permission mode, the directory-served variant and validation notes.

sections.title: Point the runtime at your app

blocks.text: Replace the sample app.softn in the deployed directory and edit runtime.config.json next to it. The entry always reads its adjacent configuration: query parameters, hashes, file drops and messages cannot replace the chosen app.

blocks.code:
{
  "version": 1,
  "id": "my-application",
  "title": "My application",
  "bundle": "./app.softn",
  "loadingText": "Loading…",
  "theme": "dark"
}
blocks.caption: A minimal runtime.config.json.

items.description: The configuration format; always 1.

The deployment’s stable identity. Local records are keyed by the configuration file’s path plus this value, so keep it the same across updates of the same app and use a different one for a different app.
The document title shown by the browser.
Where the .softn file is, relative to the configuration file. It must be same-origin HTTP(S); redirects, credentials in URLs and fragments are refused.
The text shown with the spinner while the app loads.
The initial theme, light or dark.

Optional path to a same-origin JSON permission declaration, for example ./permission.json. When present it is authoritative; otherwise the runtime uses the bundle’s permission.json, then its legacy manifest declaration, then no permissions. An invalid declaration stops loading.
Optional pin of the exact bundle bytes. Required for the preapproved permission mode.

"prompt" (the default) loads the app with capabilities withheld and shows an unbranded permission bar; "preapproved" enables the declared capabilities immediately for a trusted app and needs a valid sha256 pin.
Only when a directory serves this shell for a published app: the same-origin runs and storage endpoints; the app reaches the second as `softn.storage.*`. A standalone deployment leaves it out.

"app" (the default) pins the app to the viewport and scrolls inside it, for an app that lays out its own screen; "page" lets the document grow and scroll, for an app that reads as a long page. Only the shell changes; the bundle is the same.

Optional path to a same-origin JavaScript module whose default export returns the function the app’s `softn.backend.call(action, input, callback)` reaches. It is for actions that need something only the host should hold, such as a key or a live connection. A named module that fails to load stops the page rather than running without it.

blocks.text: Any other key is refused. Limits: the configuration is capped at 16 KiB, a sidecar permission declaration at 64 KiB and the compressed bundle at 32 MiB; the shared bundle validator also applies its entry and decompression limits, and startup fetches are bounded to 60 seconds.

In prompt mode the app is interactive straight away while a compact bar above it lists the requested access, with expandable details, Allow and Not now. The bar takes its own space rather than covering the app. Dismissing it leaves access disabled and keeps a Review permissions control available without restarting. Allowing updates the runtime’s permission configuration; scripts may reinitialise so startup features can retry.

Consent is scoped to the configuration location, the exact bundle digest and the full permission declaration: changing the app or its host restrictions asks again. Browser camera and microphone prompts stay independent, and the runtime cannot bypass the browser’s own file selection.

blocks.title: Preapproved is a deployment decision
blocks.text: Setting "permissionMode": "preapproved" belongs in runtime.config.json, not in the app manifest. It preserves declared host and file scope restrictions, writes no visitor consent record and requires the sha256 pin, so a swapped bundle is not silently trusted.

The general bundle loader isolates apps by digest; this runtime keys local records by the configuration path plus id, not by the app’s display name. Keep those stable and an updated bundle still sees its records; bundle seeding never overwrites existing records.

Test an update with disposable records before changing a live deployment. Confirm the new version opens the same data and check how schema or seed changes affect an existing user. Manifest-defined server synchronisation is not enabled automatically by this host.

sections.title: Three ways to ship one app

sections.title: When an app needs a server

blocks.text: A local app does not need a backend. A server becomes useful when records are shared under authentication, when a private service credential is needed, or when an operation must be controlled outside the editable client.

The repository has two server hosts that run server-side `.logic` with SQLite: the Rust private backend (`apps/softn-host-rust`) and the PHP host (`apps/softn-host-php`), which the single-app backend archives package. Server logic is JavaScript on both; Python is client logic only. FormLogic is a separate connected host with its own configuration.

blocks.text: The PHP-served single-app archive keeps the original bundle outside the public directory. That is useful deployment hygiene, but anything sent to a browser remains inspectable.

blocks.title: Review the public output
blocks.text: Before deploying, inspect both the downloadable client bundle and the public web directory. Keep private server scripts, credentials and databases out of client downloads.

Start with a few named operations whose inputs, outputs and authorisation rules are easy to state. A planner might need a create-task operation and a list-visible-tasks operation, with the server deciding what the signed-in person can see.

Client logic calls such an operation with `softn.backend.call(action, input, callback)`, in JavaScript or Python. The operation names are yours, and what answers the call depends on the host: its server logic, a single-app host module or FormLogic.

pages.title: SoftN and FormLogic
pages.summary: Understand the difference between exporting an editable starter and running an authenticated connected workspace.

seo.title: SoftN and FormLogic | SoftN Docs
seo.description: SoftN and FormLogic: editable starter exports with local XDB, connected iframe apps, softn.backend.call and named backend actions owned by the host, and engine choice.

blocks.text: SoftN supplies the editable app and runtime. FormLogic is a hosted workspace for forms, records, backend actions and app databases. Connecting them does not remove the client-server boundary.

There are two integration paths: converting a supported form into a local-first starter app, and running an app as a connected workspace under FormLogic. Choose the path before assuming what an export contains.
The FormLogic adapter converts supported form schemas into editable `.softn` bundles. The starter keeps its data in local XDB with sync off, and leaves out responses, credentials and access grants.
A starter is an app structure, not a copy of a live account or a connection to the original form’s private data. Inspect it, customise it and test its local record workflow.

blocks.title: An export is not an access grant
blocks.text: Downloading the client does not transfer permission to a live FormLogic backend.

The connected host renders app source in an isolated iframe. Client logic calls named backend actions with `softn.backend.call(action, input, callback)`, while the parent host owns authentication and applies the app’s permissions.

Action names and input shapes belong to the workspace, so check them in its source for the version you deploy. A workspace owner can also choose ZIPP’s smaller JavaScript-only engine; a Python app is refused there by name.

`examples/formlogic-workspace` and `examples/aokie-workspace` are editable workspace apps. Aokie’s brings calls, appointments, messages, follow-ups and transcripts into one interface, while the communication services stay part of the host integration.
A workspace example shows a client experience. Downloading the bundle does not provision telephony, authenticated records or the external services it displays.

sections.title: Keep server resources on the hosting platform

blocks.text: For custom server logic and SQLite, configure those resources on the hosting platform and expose the operations the client needs. Keep private scripts, credentials and databases on the server.

FormLogic fetches verified ZIPP engine bytes once per page and gives each isolated execution context its own copy, instance, memory and permissions. Shared engine delivery is not a shared app-data context.

sections.title: The browser engine comes from a ZIPP release

blocks.text: The engine is not committed. `packages/@softn/core/wasm-zipp` is installed from the ZIPP release that the `zipp-vm` tag in `apps/softn-host-rust/Cargo.toml` names, today v0.0.21, and verified against that release’s SHA256SUMS, so a browser build needs no Rust toolchain. The build, test, typecheck and licence scripts install it when it is missing, and `SOURCE.json` records its provenance and checksums. `packages/@softn/core/src/runtime/vm-adapter.ts` is where the engine is selected. The separate `build:zipp-wasm` workspace script builds an unreleased engine for local experiments only; no release accepts it, and it needs the matching Rust, wasm-bindgen and optimisation tooling.

pages.title: SoftN frequently asked questions
pages.summary: Straight answers about the app format, accounts, AI, local data, hosting, JavaScript and Python.

seo.title: SoftN frequently asked questions | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Answers to common SoftN questions: .softn files, AI providers, Builder, Runtime, local data, hosting, FormLogic, JavaScript and Python logic, and torch.

blocks.text: An open-source UI language, visual builder and runtime for editable web and desktop apps. A `.softn` bundle brings the interface, logic, data seeds and assets together so the app can be reopened and customised.

A ZIP-based portable app bundle. It usually holds `manifest.json`, `permission.json`, UI source, logic in JavaScript or Python, optional XDB seeds and assets. The manifest needs only a name and a main entry; Builder and Studio write the rest for you.

sections.title: Do I need an AI account?

blocks.text: No. You can try Fieldnotes, build in Builder, open Studio’s examples or write source by hand without one. Studio’s generation uses a provider you choose: Anthropic, any OpenAI-compatible service or a local model. A hosted provider can have its own credentials, limits and charges.

sections.title: Do I have to write code?

blocks.text: Builder offers visual design, data modelling and preview, and Studio can generate a starting point. Source stays available for behaviour that needs direct editing. It is fairer to promise an editable visual-and-code workflow than an app that never needs code.

XDB keeps app-scoped local records through the host, which decides persistence, native storage and sync. A connected backend can keep separate server-owned records. Bundle seeds and someone’s live records are not the same thing.

The browser library shows offline readiness for saved apps. A particular app may still depend on remote assets or backend operations, so test its real workflow without a connection before relying on it.
It is JavaScript, but it runs inside the ZIPP engine with the APIs the host exposes. There is no unrestricted DOM access, no Node.js API and no automatic support for npm packages.

sections.title: Can I write logic in Python?

blocks.text: Yes. Link a `.py` file with `<logic src>`, or choose Python in Builder’s new-project dialog or Studio’s brief. Top-level names are state, functions assign them with `global`, and `import softn` reaches host capabilities. An app uses one language, and server logic stays JavaScript.

sections.title: Can an app do machine learning?

blocks.text: Yes, on a small scale. A Python app can declare torch in its manifest and train models on the CPU in the browser, with tensors, autograd, `torch.nn` and optimizers. It is ZIPP’s torch subset, not a GPU environment.

sections.title: Can I put an app on its own domain?

blocks.text: Yes, with the single-app runtime. Configure its `runtime.config.json`, keep the deployment identity stable, and keep any private backend resources apart from the public client.
No. It is an optional connected host. FormLogic can export local-first starter apps, and it can run authenticated workspaces that call named backend actions.

sections.title: Can I hide an API key in the bundle?

blocks.text: No. Treat every client bundle as inspectable. Keep service credentials on a server and expose only the authorised operations the client needs. A custom domain or a private source archive does not make material sent to a browser secret.
Yes, under the Apache-2.0 licence. When redistributing a complete app or deployment, also review its assets, dependencies and notices, which may have their own terms.

sections.title: Are these docs a complete API specification?

blocks.text: No. They cover workflows and concepts, checked against the repository source, with links to the underlying files. They are not an exhaustive property reference; check the exact version you deploy for host configuration details.
